questions.subject: Physics
questions.stem: An athlete runs along a semicircular track of radius $R = 14\text{ m}$ from point $A$ to point $B$ across the diameter. What are the total distance traveled and the magnitude of the athlete's displacement vector? (Take $\pi = \frac{22}{7}$)

system_parameters.system_boundary: Single point-mass athlete
system_parameters.reference_frame: Inertial ground frame with origin at center O of semicircle

qrt_contract.protected_work_W: Distinguishing the scalar curved arc path integral pi*R from the vector end-to-end diameter 2R.

rival_demands.rejection_rationale: Requires geometric evaluation of circumference arc vs diameter, not bare recall.

A.diagnostic: Correct: Distance is the curved arc length pi*R = 44 m; displacement is the straight-line diameter 2R = 28 m.

B.diagnostic: Equated displacement magnitude with distance traveled, ignoring the straight-line shortcut.

C.diagnostic: Swapped the definitions of distance and displacement.

D.diagnostic: Used the full circle perimeter 2*pi*R = 88 m instead of the semicircle arc.

progressive_hints.title: Decisive Physical Invariant
progressive_hints.prompt_question: What fundamental difference distinguishes total distance from displacement vector magnitude?
progressive_hints.reveal_text: Distance is the scalar cumulative path length along the curved track ($s = \int ds$), whereas displacement magnitude is the straight-line chord length between initial and final points ($|\Delta\vec{r}| = |\vec{r}_B - \vec{r}_A|$).

progressive_hints.title: Geometric Representation
progressive_hints.prompt_question: What geometric formulae correspond to a semicircular arc and its diametric endpoints?
progressive_hints.reveal_text: For a semicircle of radius $R$: arc path length is $\pi R$, and diameter chord length is $2R$.

progressive_hints.title: First Mathematical Pivot
progressive_hints.prompt_question: What numerical values result for $R = 14\text{ m}$ with $\pi = 22/7$?
progressive_hints.reveal_text: Distance $= \frac{22}{7} \times 14 = 44\text{ m}$; Displacement magnitude $= 2 \times 14 = 28\text{ m}$.

reasoning_ladder.understand: Athlete runs from $A$ to $B$ along semicircle of radius $R = 14\text{ m}$. Goal: total distance and displacement magnitude.
reasoning_ladder.represent: Set origin at center $O$. Start $A = (-R, 0)$, End $B = (+R, 0)$. Path is the upper semicircular arc.
reasoning_ladder.connect: Distance $s = \pi R$. Displacement vector $\Delta\vec{r} = \vec{r}_B - \vec{r}_A = (+R\hat{i}) - (-R\hat{i}) = +2R\hat{i}$. Magnitude $|\Delta\vec{r}| = 2R$.
reasoning_ladder.calculate: Distance $= \frac{22}{7} \times 14 = 44\text{ m}$. Displacement $= 2 \times 14 = 28\text{ m}$.
reasoning_ladder.interpret: Distance ($44\text{ m}$) strictly exceeds displacement magnitude ($28\text{ m}$) because the path is curved, satisfying $|\Delta\vec{r}| \le s$.

derivation_steps: Athlete travels along the circumference of a semicircle: $s = \pi R = \frac{22}{7} \times 14\text{ m} = 44\text{ m}$.
Displacement is the vector connecting start point A to end point B: $\Delta\vec{r} = \vec{r}_B - \vec{r}_A$.
Points A and B are diametrically opposite on the circle, so the straight-line distance is the diameter: $|\Delta\vec{r}| = 2R = 2 \times 14\text{ m} = 28\text{ m}$.

limiting_cases.expected: Distance -> 0 m and Displacement -> 0 m (Point limit)

limiting_cases.condition: Full round trip (Athlete continues back to A)
limiting_cases.expected: Distance = 2 pi R = 88 m; Displacement = 0 m

independent_check.quick_check: Displacement is always the shortest path between two points; $28\text{ m} < 44\text{ m}$ strictly satisfies $|\Delta\vec{r}| \le s$.
independent_check.check_it_another_way: Ratio $\frac{s}{|\Delta\vec{r}|} = \frac{\pi R}{2R} = \frac{\pi}{2} \approx 1.571$. Here $44 / 28 = 11/7 \approx 1.571$. Exactly consistent.
independent_check.watch_out: Do not confuse displacement (which depends only on endpoints) with distance (which depends on the full trajectory history).
independent_check.review_this_idea: Core 1: KIN-01 (Distance vs Displacement Invariant)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.stem: A car travels the first half of a total distance $d$ at a uniform speed of $30\text{ km/h}$ and the remaining half of the distance at a uniform speed of $60\text{ km/h}$. What is the average speed of the car for the entire journey?

system_parameters.system_boundary: Single automobile moving in a 1D straight line
system_parameters.reference_frame: Ground frame (+x along direction of motion)

qrt_contract.protected_work_W: Modeling average speed as total distance over total time, arriving at the harmonic mean rather than arithmetic mean.

rival_demands.rejection_rationale: Requires algebraic rate modeling across unequal time segments.

A.diagnostic: Correct: Applied harmonic mean: v_avg = 2*v1*v2 / (v1 + v2) = 2(30)(60) / 90 = 40 km/h.

B.diagnostic: Arithmetic mean trap: evaluated (30 + 60) / 2 = 45 km/h, ignoring that the car spends twice as much time at 30 km/h.

C.diagnostic: Guessed midpoint between 40 and 60 km/h.

D.diagnostic: Applied incorrect geometric/harmonic calculation yielding 36 km/h.

progressive_hints.title: Decisive Physical Invariant
progressive_hints.prompt_question: What is the inviolable definition of average speed for any journey?
progressive_hints.reveal_text: Average speed is defined as total distance divided by total elapsed time: $v_{\text{avg}} = \frac{d_{\text{total}}}{t_{\text{total}}}$, NOT the simple average of speeds.

progressive_hints.title: Time Segment Representation
progressive_hints.prompt_question: Letting the total distance be $d$, how much time does each half-distance segment take?

progressive_hints.title: First Mathematical Pivot
progressive_hints.prompt_question: What is the total time $t_{\text{total}} = t_1 + t_2$, and what average speed does it yield?
progressive_hints.reveal_text: $t_{\text{total}} = \frac{d}{60} + \frac{d}{120} = \frac{3d}{120} = \frac{d}{40} \implies v_{\text{avg}} = \frac{d}{d/40} = 40\text{ km/h}$.

reasoning_ladder.understand: Car travels first half of distance at $v_1 = 30\text{ km/h}$ and second half at $v_2 = 60\text{ km/h}$. Goal: average speed $v_{\text{avg}}$.
reasoning_ladder.represent: Divide total distance $d$ into two equal segments $s_1 = d/2$ and $s_2 = d/2$. Times are $t_1 = s_1/v_1$ and $t_2 = s_2/v_2$.
reasoning_ladder.connect: By definition, $v_{\text{avg}} = \frac{d}{t_1 + t_2} = \frac{d}{\frac{d}{2v_1} + \frac{d}{2v_2}} = \frac{2}{\frac{1}{v_1} + \frac{1}{v_2}} = \frac{2v_1 v_2}{v_1 + v_2}$ (Harmonic Mean).
reasoning_ladder.interpret: Because the car spends twice as much time at $30\text{ km/h}$ ($t_1 = 2 t_2$), the time-weighted average is pulled toward $30\text{ km/h}$, yielding $40\text{ km/h} < 45\text{ km/h}$.

derivation_steps: Let total distance be $d$. Each half has length $s = d/2$.

limiting_cases.condition: v1 -> 0 (Vehicle breaks down on first half)

independent_check.quick_check: Harmonic mean is always strictly less than arithmetic mean for distinct positive speeds: $40\text{ km/h} < 45\text{ km/h}$. Physically sound.
independent_check.check_it_another_way: Time ratio: $t_1 : t_2 = \frac{d/2}{30} : \frac{d/2}{60} = 2 : 1$. Average speed is $\frac{2(30) + 1(60)}{2 + 1} = \frac{120}{3} = 40\text{ km/h}$. Exact match.
independent_check.watch_out: Never use $(v_1 + v_2)/2$ for equal DISTANCES; arithmetic mean applies ONLY to equal TIMES.
independent_check.review_this_idea: Core 1: KIN-03 (Weighted Kinematic Averages: Harmonic vs Arithmetic Mean)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.stem: A tennis ball is projected vertically upward into the air. At the exact instant the ball reaches its highest point (apex), what are its instantaneous velocity and instantaneous acceleration? (Take upward as positive and magnitude of gravitational acceleration as $g = 9.8\text{ m/s}^2$)

system_parameters.system_boundary: Isolated tennis ball under gravitational field
system_parameters.reference_frame: Inertial ground frame with upward chosen as positive (+y)

qrt_contract.protected_work_W: Decoupling instantaneous state of rest (v = 0) from the constant gravitational force field producing uninterrupted downward acceleration a = -g.

rival_demands.rejection_rationale: Requires applying physical definition of acceleration as rate of velocity change at a turning point.

A.diagnostic: Correct: At apex, velocity changes sign so v = 0; gravity acts continuously so a = -g = -9.8 m/s².

B.diagnostic: Classic apex fallacy: assumed that because the ball momentarily stops (v = 0), acceleration must also be zero (which would mean it hovers forever).

C.diagnostic: Conflated acceleration value with velocity.

D.diagnostic: Inverted acceleration sign: gravity points downward (-y), not upward.

progressive_hints.title: Decisive Physical Invariant
progressive_hints.prompt_question: What is the defining kinematic condition that marks the highest point of a vertical trajectory?
progressive_hints.reveal_text: The apex is the turning point where the vertical velocity changes sign from positive (upward) to negative (downward), meaning instantaneous velocity is strictly $v = 0$.

progressive_hints.title: Gravitational Field Representation
progressive_hints.prompt_question: Does the Earth's gravitational pull shut off when the ball reaches the top?
progressive_hints.reveal_text: No. The downward gravitational force $F = mg$ acts without interruption throughout the entire flight, producing constant downward acceleration: $\vec{a} = -g\hat{j}$.

progressive_hints.title: First Logical Constraint
progressive_hints.prompt_question: Why would acceleration being zero at the top violate observation?
progressive_hints.reveal_text: If $a = 0$ while $v = 0$, Newton's First Law requires the ball to remain at rest indefinitely, hovering permanently in mid-air!

reasoning_ladder.understand: Ball projected vertically under gravity ($g = 9.8\text{ m/s}^2$). Target: instantaneous velocity and acceleration at highest point.
reasoning_ladder.represent: Choose vertical axis $+y$ pointing upward. Trajectory is $y(t) = v_0 t - \frac{1}{2}gt^2$. Velocity is $v(t) = \frac{dy}{dt} = v_0 - gt$. Acceleration is $a(t) = \frac{dv}{dt} = -g$.
reasoning_ladder.connect: The highest point occurs when $\frac{dy}{dt} = 0 \implies v = 0$. Acceleration is $a = \frac{dv}{dt} = -g = -9.8\text{ m/s}^2$.
reasoning_ladder.calculate: At apex: $v = 0\text{ m/s}$, $a = -9.8\text{ m/s}^2$.
reasoning_ladder.interpret: Velocity is zero at a single isolated instant, but its rate of change (acceleration) is $-9.8\text{ m/s}^2$, pulling the ball back downward immediately.

derivation_steps: Establish vertical coordinate $+y$ pointing upward: position $y(t) = y_0 + v_0 t - \frac{1}{2}gt^2$.
Differentiate to find velocity: $v(t) = \dot{y}(t) = v_0 - gt$.

limiting_cases.condition: Instant just before apex (t = t_apex - epsilon)
Instant just after apex (t = t_apex + epsilon)

independent_check.quick_check: On an $x-t$ graph, the apex is a local maximum: slope (velocity) is zero, but concavity (second derivative / acceleration) is strictly negative ($-g$).
independent_check.check_it_another_way: Newton II check: only force acting is gravity $F_g = -mg$. Therefore $a = F_g / m = -mg / m = -g = -9.8\text{ m/s}^2$ everywhere in flight.
independent_check.watch_out: Never conflate the value of a function ($v = 0$) with the value of its derivative ($dv/dt = -g$).
independent_check.review_this_idea: Core 1: KIN-07 (Vertical Free Fall & Apex Invariants)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.stem: A steel ball is released from rest from the top of a tall tower. It falls freely under gravity. What is the ratio of the vertical distances fallen by the ball in the 1st second, the 2nd second, and the 3rd second of its motion?

system_parameters.system_boundary: Steel ball falling freely under gravity
system_parameters.reference_frame: Inertial ground frame with downward chosen as positive (+y)

qrt_contract.protected_work_W: Evaluating interval displacement s_n = s(n) - s(n-1) = 1/2 g (2n - 1) to derive Galileo's law of odd numbers.

rival_demands.rejection_rationale: Requires interval difference subtraction of quadratic positions.

A.diagnostic: Correct: Galileo's law of odd numbers gives s_1 : s_2 : s_3 = 1 : 3 : 5.

B.diagnostic: Linear fallacy: assumed distances scale linearly with time as 1 : 2 : 3.

C.diagnostic: Reported cumulative distances from start y(1) : y(2) : y(3) = 1 : 4 : 9 instead of individual 1-second intervals.

D.diagnostic: Took square root of time intervals erroneously.

progressive_hints.title: Decisive Physical Invariant
progressive_hints.prompt_question: What formula gives the cumulative vertical distance fallen from rest after time $t$ under gravity?
progressive_hints.reveal_text: Cumulative distance from rest: $y(t) = \frac{1}{2}gt^2$.

progressive_hints.title: Interval Displacement Representation
progressive_hints.prompt_question: How do you calculate the distance fallen during the $n^{\text{th}}$ second (between $t = n-1$ and $t = n$)?
progressive_hints.reveal_text: Subtract consecutive cumulative distances: $\Delta y_n = y(n) - y(n-1) = \frac{1}{2}g [n^2 - (n-1)^2] = \frac{1}{2}g(2n - 1)$.

progressive_hints.title: First Mathematical Pivot
progressive_hints.prompt_question: What ratio results for $n = 1, 2, 3$?

reasoning_ladder.understand: Ball released from rest ($u = 0$) under gravity $g$. Goal: ratio of distances fallen in 1st, 2nd, and 3rd seconds.
reasoning_ladder.represent: Define downward vertical coordinate $y$. Cumulative distance from rest: $y(t) = \frac{1}{2}gt^2$.
reasoning_ladder.connect: Distance in $n^{\text{th}}$ second is $\Delta y_n = y(n) - y(n-1) = \frac{1}{2}g(2n - 1)$.
reasoning_ladder.interpret: In equal consecutive time intervals from rest, a uniformly accelerating body traverses distances proportional to successive odd integers.

derivation_steps: Distance in 2nd second: $\Delta y_2 = y_2 - y_1 = 2g - \frac{1}{2}g = \frac{3}{2}g$.
Distance in 3rd second: $\Delta y_3 = y_3 - y_2 = \frac{9}{2}g - 2g = \frac{5}{2}g$.

limiting_cases.condition: Sum of first n odd numbers

independent_check.quick_check: Cumulative distances are $1, 1+3=4, 1+3+5=9$, matching $1^2, 2^2, 3^2$. Exact mathematical identity.
independent_check.check_it_another_way: Use average velocity in each second: in 1st second, $v_{\text{avg}} = 0.5g$; in 2nd second, $v_{\text{avg}} = 1.5g$; in 3rd second, $v_{\text{avg}} = 2.5g$. Ratio of distances is $0.5 : 1.5 : 2.5 = 1 : 3 : 5$.
independent_check.watch_out: Do not confuse cumulative distance ($1 : 4 : 9$) with individual interval distance ($1 : 3 : 5$).
independent_check.review_this_idea: Core 1: KIN-05 (Constant Acceleration Equation Selection: Galileo's Odd-Number Rule)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.stem: The velocity-time graph of a particle moving along a straight line is shown in Figure KIN-02. The particle accelerates uniformly from rest to $v = 20\text{ m/s}$ in $t = 5\text{ s}$, cruises at constant speed of $20\text{ m/s}$ for $10\text{ s}$, and decelerates uniformly to rest in $5\text{ s}$. What is the total displacement of the particle, and what is its average velocity over the entire $20\text{ s}$ journey?

system_parameters.system_boundary: 1D particle moving along straight track

qrt_contract.protected_work_W: Evaluating trapezoidal area under v-t graph Area = 1/2 * (b1 + b2) * h = 1/2 * (20 + 10) * 20 = 300 m and computing v_avg = 300 / 20 = 15 m/s.

rival_demands.rejection_rationale: Requires multi-phase graphic representation and geometric calculus.

A.diagnostic: Correct: Trapezoid area = 0.5 * (20 + 10) * 20 = 300 m; v_avg = 300 / 20 = 15.0 m/s.

B.diagnostic: Treated whole motion as constant speed cruise: evaluated 20 * 20 = 400 m, v_avg = 20 m/s.

C.diagnostic: Miscomputed trapezoid bases: evaluated 0.5 * (20 + 5) * 20 = 250 m.

D.diagnostic: Treated whole graph as triangle: evaluated 0.5 * 20 * 20 = 200 m.

progressive_hints.title: Decisive Physical Invariant
progressive_hints.prompt_question: What geometric operation on a velocity-time graph yields the total displacement?
progressive_hints.reveal_text: The total displacement is the area under the velocity-time graph: $\Delta x = \int v(t) dt$.

progressive_hints.title: Trapezoidal Geometry Representation
progressive_hints.prompt_question: What are the two parallel bases and height of the trapezoid formed by this velocity profile?
progressive_hints.reveal_text: Bottom base $b_1 = 20\text{ s}$ (from $t = 0$ to $20\text{ s}$); top base $b_2 = 10\text{ s}$ (from $t = 5$ to $15\text{ s}$); height $h = 20\text{ m/s}$.

progressive_hints.title: First Mathematical Pivot
progressive_hints.prompt_question: What formula calculates the trapezoidal area and average velocity?
progressive_hints.reveal_text: $\text{Area} = \frac{1}{2}(b_1 + b_2)h = \frac{1}{2}(20 + 10)(20) = 300\text{ m}$, and $v_{\text{avg}} = \frac{300\text{ m}}{20\text{ s}} = 15.0\text{ m/s}$.

reasoning_ladder.understand: Particle accelerates from 0 to $20\text{ m/s}$ in $5\text{ s}$, cruises for $10\text{ s}$ ($t = 5$ to $15\text{ s}$), decelerates to rest in $5\text{ s}$ ($t = 15$ to $20\text{ s}$). Goal: displacement and $v_{\text{avg}}$.
reasoning_ladder.represent: The $v-t$ curve forms a symmetric trapezoid. Base $b_1 = 20\text{ s}$, top base $b_2 = 15 - 5 = 10\text{ s}$, height $v_{\text{max}} = 20\text{ m/s}$.
reasoning_ladder.connect: Displacement is trapezoidal area: $\Delta x = \frac{1}{2}(b_1 + b_2)v_{\text{max}}$. Average velocity: $v_{\text{avg}} = \frac{\Delta x}{t_{\text{total}}}$.
reasoning_ladder.interpret: The particle covers $300\text{ m}$ in $20\text{ s}$, giving an average velocity of $15.0\text{ m/s}$, which is reasonably below the peak cruising speed of $20\text{ m/s}$.

derivation_steps: Phase 2 displacement (constant speed rectangle): $\Delta x_2 = (10)(20) = 200\text{ m}$.
Average velocity: $v_{\text{avg}} = \frac{\Delta x}{t_{\text{total}}} = \frac{300\text{ m}}{20\text{ s}} = 15.0\text{ m/s}$.

independent_check.quick_check: Average velocity must lie between 0 and peak speed ($0 < v_{\text{avg}} < 20\text{ m/s}$); $15.0\text{ m/s}$ satisfies this bound.
independent_check.check_it_another_way: Use trapezoid formula: $\frac{20 + 10}{2} \times 20 = 300\text{ m}$. Sum of parts: $50 + 200 + 50 = 300\text{ m}$. Exact match.
independent_check.watch_out: Do not average the three phase velocities $(10 + 20 + 10)/3 = 13.33\text{ m/s}$; time weighting must be preserved.
independent_check.review_this_idea: Core 1: KIN-11 (Motion Graphs & Geometric Calculus: Trapezoidal Area)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.stem: A marksman fires a rifle horizontally at $u = 200\text{ m/s}$ from the edge of a cliff of height $h = 20.0\text{ m}$ above a level plain. Simultaneously, an identical bullet is dropped from rest from the same height. Taking $g = 10.0\text{ m/s}^2$ and neglecting air resistance, what are the flight times of the two bullets, and how far from the base of the cliff does the fired bullet land?

system_parameters.system_boundary: Two identical bullets under 2D projectile kinematics
system_parameters.reference_frame: Inertial ground frame with origin at cliff base

options.A: Both land at $t = 2.0\text{ s}$; fired bullet lands $400\text{ m}$ from cliff base
options.B: Fired bullet lands at $t = 1.0\text{ s}$; dropped bullet lands at $t = 2.0\text{ s}$
options.C: Both land at $t = 2.0\text{ s}$; fired bullet lands $200\text{ m}$ from cliff base
options.D: Fired bullet lands at $t = 4.0\text{ s}$; dropped bullet lands at $t = 2.0\text{ s}$

qrt_contract.protected_work_W: Recognizing independence of perpendicular motions: horizontal velocity does not affect vertical drop time t = sqrt(2h/g) = 2.0 s, giving horizontal range x = u*t = 400 m.

rival_demands.rejection_rationale: Requires modeling independence of orthogonal kinematic components.

A.diagnostic: Correct: Both bullets fall under identical vertical acceleration with u_y = 0, so t = sqrt(2h/g) = 2.0 s; horizontal range is x = u*t = 200 * 2.0 = 400 m.

B.diagnostic: Assumed fired bullet lands sooner due to high speed.

C.diagnostic: Failed to multiply horizontal velocity by full flight time of 2 seconds.

D.diagnostic: Assumed horizontal motion extends flight time, taking twice as long.

progressive_hints.title: Decisive Physical Invariant
progressive_hints.prompt_question: Does horizontal velocity affect the vertical acceleration or vertical fall time of an object in a uniform gravity field?
progressive_hints.reveal_text: No. Perpendicular kinematic motions are completely independent: gravity acts purely vertically ($a_y = -g$), so horizontal motion does not alter the vertical rate of fall.

progressive_hints.title: Vertical Fall Time Representation
progressive_hints.prompt_question: What is the initial vertical velocity of both bullets, and what formula gives their flight time from height $h$?
progressive_hints.reveal_text: Both have zero initial vertical velocity ($u_y = 0$). Vertical fall time is $t = \sqrt{\frac{2h}{g}} = \sqrt{\frac{2(20.0)}{10.0}} = \sqrt{4.0} = 2.0\text{ s}$.

progressive_hints.title: First Mathematical Pivot
progressive_hints.prompt_question: What horizontal distance does the fired bullet travel during this $2.0\text{ s}$ interval?
progressive_hints.reveal_text: $x = u_x \cdot t = 200\text{ m/s} \times 2.0\text{ s} = 400\text{ m}$.

reasoning_ladder.understand: Bullet 1 fired horizontally at $u = 200\text{ m/s}$ from $h = 20.0\text{ m}$. Bullet 2 dropped from rest. $g = 10.0\text{ m/s}^2$. Goal: flight times and horizontal range.
reasoning_ladder.represent: Choose origin at cliff base: $+x$ horizontal, $+y$ vertical upward. Initial positions $(0, h)$. Bullet 1: $\vec{u}_1 = 200\hat{i}$. Bullet 2: $\vec{u}_2 = 0$. Acceleration for both: $\vec{a} = -g\hat{j}$.
reasoning_ladder.connect: Vertical motion is identical for both: $y(t) = h - \frac{1}{2}gt^2 = 0 \implies t = \sqrt{\frac{2h}{g}}$. Horizontal motion for fired bullet: $x(t) = u_x t$.
reasoning_ladder.calculate: $t = \sqrt{\frac{2(20.0)}{10.0}} = 2.0\text{ s}$ for both bullets. Horizontal range: $x = 200 \times 2.0 = 400\text{ m}$.
reasoning_ladder.interpret: Both bullets hit the ground simultaneously because gravity pulls downward independently of horizontal velocity; the fired bullet lands $400\text{ m}$ away.

derivation_steps: Vertical equation of motion: $y(t) = h + u_y t - \frac{1}{2}gt^2$.
For both bullets, initial vertical velocity is zero: $u_y = 0$.
Horizontal motion is uniform ($a_x = 0$): $x = u_x t = 200\text{ m/s} \times 2.0\text{ s} = 400\text{ m}$.

limiting_cases.expected: x = 0 m, t = 2.0 s (Pure vertical drop)

independent_check.quick_check: Final vertical velocity at impact: $v_y = -gt = -10(2) = -20\text{ m/s}$. Both bullets strike the ground with the exact same vertical speed.
independent_check.check_it_another_way: Total impact speed for fired bullet: $v = \sqrt{u_x^2 + v_y^2} = \sqrt{200^2 + 20^2} = \sqrt{40400} \approx 201\text{ m/s}$. Energy check: $\frac{1}{2}mv^2 - \frac{1}{2}mu^2 = \frac{1}{2}m(400) = m(10)(20) = mgh$. Conserved.
independent_check.watch_out: Do not believe that horizontal speed 'carries' or 'floats' the bullet; vertical acceleration is strictly $-g$ at all times.
independent_check.review_this_idea: Core 1: KIN-08 (2D Projectile Component Decoupling: Independence of Motions)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.stem: A ball is thrown vertically upward from the ground with an initial speed $u$. It is observed to pass a window at a height $h = 40.0\text{ m}$ above the ground at two instants: $t_1 = 2.0\text{ s}$ on its way up, and $t_2 = 4.0\text{ s}$ on its way down. Taking $g = 10.0\text{ m/s}^2$, what was the initial launch speed $u$, and what maximum height $H_{\text{max}}$ above the ground does the ball reach?

system_parameters.system_boundary: Ball in 1D vertical free fall

qrt_contract.protected_work_W: Using Vieta's relations on the quadratic 1/2 g t^2 - u t + h = 0 to establish t1 + t2 = 2u/g => u = g(t1 + t2)/2 = 30 m/s and H_max = u^2 / (2g) = 45 m.

rival_demands.rejection_rationale: Requires quadratic equation root analysis and parabolic symmetry deduction.

A.diagnostic: Correct: Vieta's sum t1 + t2 = 2u/g => u = 10(6)/2 = 30 m/s; H_max = u^2 / (2g) = 900 / 20 = 45.0 m.

B.diagnostic: Assumed height h = 40 m is the maximum height, giving u = sqrt(2gh) = 28.3 m/s rounded erroneously.

C.diagnostic: Found u = 30 m/s correctly but calculated H_max as u^2 / g = 60 m instead of u^2 / (2g).

D.diagnostic: Overestimated launch speed to 40 m/s.

progressive_hints.title: Decisive Physical Invariant
progressive_hints.prompt_question: What quadratic equation in time $t$ gives the instances when a vertical projectile is at height $h$?
progressive_hints.reveal_text: Position formula: $h = ut - \frac{1}{2}gt^2 \implies \frac{1}{2}gt^2 - ut + h = 0$.

progressive_hints.title: Vieta's Sum of Roots Representation
progressive_hints.prompt_question: What is the sum of the two roots $t_1 + t_2$ of this quadratic equation, and how does it relate to $u$?
progressive_hints.reveal_text: By Vieta's formulas, the sum of roots is $t_1 + t_2 = \frac{u}{g/2} = \frac{2u}{g}$. This equals the total time of flight back to the ground!

progressive_hints.title: First Mathematical Pivot
progressive_hints.prompt_question: What are $u$ and maximum height $H_{\text{max}}$, given $t_1 = 2.0\text{ s}$ and $t_2 = 4.0\text{ s}$?

reasoning_ladder.understand: Vertical projectile passes $h = 40.0\text{ m}$ at $t_1 = 2.0\text{ s}$ and $t_2 = 4.0\text{ s}$. Goal: launch speed $u$ and max height $H_{\text{max}}$.
reasoning_ladder.represent: Choose $+y$ upward from ground. Trajectory: $y(t) = ut - \frac{1}{2}gt^2$. At $y = h$: $\frac{1}{2}gt^2 - ut + h = 0$.
reasoning_ladder.connect: By Vieta's formulas: $t_1 + t_2 = \frac{2u}{g}$, and $t_1 t_2 = \frac{2h}{g}$. Maximum height is $H_{\text{max}} = \frac{u^2}{2g}$.
reasoning_ladder.calculate: $u = \frac{g(t_1 + t_2)}{2} = \frac{10(2 + 4)}{2} = 30.0\text{ m/s}$. Check product: $t_1 t_2 = 2(4) = 8\text{ s}^2 = \frac{2(40)}{10} = 8$. Perfectly consistent! $H_{\text{max}} = \frac{30^2}{2(10)} = \frac{900}{20} = 45.0\text{ m}$.
reasoning_ladder.interpret: The apex occurs at $t_{\text{apex}} = \frac{t_1 + t_2}{2} = 3.0\text{ s}$, exactly midway between the two window transits, reaching $45.0\text{ m}$.

derivation_steps: The two roots $t_1, t_2$ represent upward and downward crossings.
Sum of roots: $t_1 + t_2 = \frac{2u}{g} \implies u = \frac{g(t_1 + t_2)}{2}$.

limiting_cases.condition: t1 = t2 (Window is at the apex)

independent_check.quick_check: Apex time is $t = 3.0\text{ s}$. Height at $3.0\text{ s}$: $y(3) = 30(3) - 5(9) = 90 - 45 = 45\text{ m} > 40\text{ m}$. Physically robust.
independent_check.check_it_another_way: Time spent above the window is $\Delta t = t_2 - t_1 = 4.0 - 2.0 = 2.0\text{ s}$. Ascent from window to apex takes $1.0\text{ s}$. Speed at window is $v = g(1.0) = 10\text{ m/s}$. Energy: $u^2 = v^2 + 2gh = 100 + 2(10)(40) = 900 \implies u = 30\text{ m/s}$.
independent_check.watch_out: Do not omit factor of 2 in denominator for maximum height ($u^2 / (2g)$, not $u^2 / g$).
independent_check.review_this_idea: Core 1: KIN-07 (Vertical Free Fall: Time Symmetry and Root Sums)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.stem: An ideal projectile is launched from ground level across a horizontal field. It is found that the horizontal range $R$ of the projectile is exactly equal to three times its maximum height $H_{\text{max}}$ ($R = 3 H_{\text{max}}$). What is the angle of projection $\theta$ above the horizontal?

system_parameters.system_boundary: 2D parabolic projectile
idealizations: Launch and landing on same horizontal plane

qrt_contract.protected_work_W: Formulating the canonical landmark invariant R = 4 H cot theta and equating to 3 H to deduce tan theta = 4/3.

rival_demands.rejection_rationale: Requires trigonometric landmark ratio formulation.

A.diagnostic: Correct: R = 4*H / tan(theta); with R = 3H, 3H = 4H / tan(theta) => tan(theta) = 4/3 => theta = arctan(4/3) approx 53.1 deg.

B.diagnostic: Inverted the tangent ratio: evaluated tan(theta) = 3/4 => theta approx 36.9 deg.

C.diagnostic: Assumed 45 deg angle where R = 4H, not 3H.

D.diagnostic: Omitted factor of 4: evaluated tan(theta) = 3.

progressive_hints.title: Decisive Physical Invariant
progressive_hints.prompt_question: What standard formulae express horizontal range $R$ and maximum height $H$ in terms of launch speed $u$, angle $\theta$, and $g$?
progressive_hints.reveal_text: $R = \frac{u^2 \sin 2\theta}{g} = \frac{2u^2 \sin\theta\cos\theta}{g}$, and $H = \frac{u^2 \sin^2\theta}{2g}$.

progressive_hints.title: Universal Landmark Ratio Representation
progressive_hints.prompt_question: What clean relationship connects $R$ and $H$ when you divide $R$ by $H$?
progressive_hints.reveal_text: $\frac{R}{H} = \frac{2\sin\theta\cos\theta}{\sin^2\theta / 2} = \frac{4\cos\theta}{\sin\theta} = \frac{4}{\tan\theta} = 4\cot\theta$.

progressive_hints.title: First Mathematical Pivot
progressive_hints.prompt_question: Given $R = 3H$, what equation solves for $\tan\theta$?
progressive_hints.reveal_text: $\frac{4}{\tan\theta} = 3 \implies \tan\theta = \frac{4}{3} \implies \theta = \arctan\left(\frac{4}{3}\right) \approx 53.1^\circ$.

reasoning_ladder.understand: Horizontal range $R$ equals three times maximum height $H$: $R = 3H$. Goal: launch angle $\theta$.
reasoning_ladder.represent: Standard projectile on horizontal plane: $R = \frac{2 u^2 \sin\theta\cos\theta}{g}$, $H = \frac{u^2 \sin^2\theta}{2g}$.
reasoning_ladder.connect: Form the landmark ratio: $\frac{R}{H} = \frac{2 u^2 \sin\theta\cos\theta / g}{u^2 \sin^2\theta / (2g)} = \frac{4}{\tan\theta}$.
reasoning_ladder.calculate: Substitute condition $\frac{R}{H} = 3$: $\frac{4}{\tan\theta} = 3 \implies \tan\theta = \frac{4}{3} \implies \theta = \arctan\left(\frac{4}{3}\right) \approx 53.13^\circ$.
reasoning_ladder.interpret: Because $R < 4H$, the launch angle must exceed $45^\circ$; $\theta \approx 53.1^\circ$ matches this physical requirement.

independent_check.quick_check: At $\theta = 45^\circ$, $R = 4H$. Since $R = 3H < 4H$, the trajectory is taller and narrower, meaning $\theta > 45^\circ$. $\arctan(4/3) \approx 53.1^\circ > 45^\circ$. Correct.
independent_check.check_it_another_way: Trajectory equation: $y = x\tan\theta - \frac{g x^2}{2u^2\cos^2\theta} = x\tan\theta(1 - x/R)$. At apex $x = R/2$: $H = \frac{R}{2}\tan\theta(1 - 1/2) = \frac{R}{4}\tan\theta \implies R = 4H/\tan\theta$. Universal identity verified.
independent_check.watch_out: Do not invert the ratio ($3/4 \implies 36.9^\circ$); smaller angles produce flatter trajectories where $R > 4H$.
independent_check.review_this_idea: Core 1: KIN-09 (Projectile Trajectory & Flight Landmarks: R = 4H cot theta)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.stem: Two projectiles are launched from the same ground origin with identical launch speed $u$, at complementary elevation angles $\theta_1$ and $\theta_2$ (where $\theta_1 + \theta_2 = 90^\circ$). If their times of flight are $T_1$ and $T_2$ and their maximum heights are $H_1$ and $H_2$, which relation connecting their horizontal range $R$ to their flight times is mathematically exact?

system_parameters.system_boundary: Two complementary projectiles launched across level horizontal ground

qrt_contract.protected_work_W: Evaluating the product T1 * T2 = (2u sin theta / g)(2u cos theta / g) = 2/g * (u^2 sin 2theta / g) = 2R/g to deduce R = 1/2 g T1 T2.

rival_demands.rejection_rationale: Requires formal algebraic product synthesis of complementary flight time formulae.

A.diagnostic: Correct: T1*T2 = (2u*sin(theta)/g)(2u*cos(theta)/g) = (2/g)(u^2*sin(2*theta)/g) = 2R/g => R = 1/2 g T1 T2.

B.diagnostic: Omitted factor of 1/2: evaluated R = g T1 T2.

C.diagnostic: Double counted factor of 2 in numerator.

D.diagnostic: Used 1/4 factor from height product erroneously.

progressive_hints.title: Decisive Physical Invariant
progressive_hints.prompt_question: What are the flight times $T_1$ and $T_2$ for complementary launch angles $\theta$ and $90^\circ - \theta$?
progressive_hints.reveal_text: $T_1 = \frac{2u\sin\theta}{g}$ and $T_2 = \frac{2u\sin(90^\circ - \theta)}{g} = \frac{2u\cos\theta}{g}$.

progressive_hints.title: Product of Flight Times Representation
progressive_hints.prompt_question: What product results when you multiply $T_1$ and $T_2$?
progressive_hints.reveal_text: $T_1 T_2 = \frac{4 u^2 \sin\theta\cos\theta}{g^2} = \frac{2}{g} \left(\frac{2u^2\sin\theta\cos\theta}{g}\right)$.

progressive_hints.title: First Mathematical Pivot
progressive_hints.prompt_question: Recognizing the common horizontal range $R = \frac{2u^2\sin\theta\cos\theta}{g}$, what is $R$ in terms of $g, T_1,$ and $T_2$?
progressive_hints.reveal_text: $T_1 T_2 = \frac{2R}{g} \implies R = \frac{1}{2} g T_1 T_2$.

reasoning_ladder.understand: Two projectiles launched at same speed $u$ at complementary angles $\theta$ and $90^\circ - \theta$. Goal: express common range $R$ in terms of $T_1$ and $T_2$.
reasoning_ladder.represent: Time of flight: $T_1 = \frac{2u\sin\theta}{g}$, $T_2 = \frac{2u\cos\theta}{g}$. Horizontal range: $R = \frac{u^2 \sin 2\theta}{g} = \frac{2u^2\sin\theta\cos\theta}{g}$.
reasoning_ladder.connect: Multiply the two flight times: $T_1 T_2 = \left(\frac{2u\sin\theta}{g}\right)\left(\frac{2u\cos\theta}{g}\right) = \frac{2}{g}\left(\frac{2u^2\sin\theta\cos\theta}{g}\right) = \frac{2R}{g}$.
reasoning_ladder.calculate: Rearrange for range: $R = \frac{1}{2} g T_1 T_2$.
reasoning_ladder.interpret: The product of flight times of complementary projectiles directly measures the horizontal ground distance traversed.

derivation_steps: Since horizontal range is $R = \frac{u^2 \sin 2\theta}{g}$, we have $T_1 T_2 = \frac{2R}{g}$.

limiting_cases.expected: T1 = T2 = sqrt(2) u/g => R = 1/2 g (2 u^2 / g^2) = u^2/g (Maximum range recovered)
T1 -> 0 => R -> 0 (Zero range on ground level)

independent_check.quick_check: Dimensional check: $[g T_1 T_2] = (\text{m/s}^2)(\text{s}^2) = \text{m}$. Perfectly homogeneous.
independent_check.check_it_another_way: Also note height product: $H_1 H_2 = \left(\frac{u^2\sin^2\theta}{2g}\right)\left(\frac{u^2\cos^2\theta}{2g}\right) = \frac{u^4 \sin^2 2\theta}{16 g^2} = \frac{R^2}{16} \implies R = 4\sqrt{H_1 H_2}$. Both classic relations are mutually consistent.
independent_check.watch_out: Do not omit the $1/2$ factor; $T_1 T_2$ carries $4/g^2$, which factors into $2/g \times (2u^2\sin\theta\cos\theta/g) = 2R/g$.
independent_check.review_this_idea: Core 1: KIN-09 (Projectile Trajectory & Flight Landmarks: Complementary Angle Product)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.stem: A test vehicle travels around a circular roundabout track of radius $R = 50.0\text{ m}$ at a constant speed of $v = 20.0\text{ m/s}$ ($72.0\text{ km/h}$). During the time interval required for the vehicle to travel halfway around the circle (from point $A$ to diametrically opposite point $B$), what are its average speed and the magnitude of its average velocity vector? (Take $\pi \approx 3.14$)

system_parameters.system_boundary: Vehicle moving along circular perimeter
system_parameters.reference_frame: Inertial ground frame with origin at roundabout center

options.A: Average speed $= 20.0\text{ m/s}$, Average velocity magnitude $= \frac{40.0}{\pi}\text{ m/s} \approx 12.7\text{ m/s}$
options.B: Average speed $= 20.0\text{ m/s}$, Average velocity magnitude $= 20.0\text{ m/s}$
options.C: Average speed $= 0\text{ m/s}$, Average velocity magnitude $= 0\text{ m/s}$
options.D: Average speed $= \frac{40.0}{\pi}\text{ m/s} \approx 12.7\text{ m/s}$, Average velocity magnitude $= 20.0\text{ m/s}$

qrt_contract.protected_work_W: Distinguishing the curved path integral (pi*R) yielding average speed from the straight diameter displacement vector (2R) yielding average velocity.

rival_demands.rejection_rationale: Requires geometric evaluation of arc length vs chord length over the elapsed flight time.

A.diagnostic: Correct: Semicircle arc length = pi*R = 50*pi m; elapsed time Delta t = (50*pi)/20 = 2.5*pi s. Average speed = (50*pi)/(2.5*pi) = 20 m/s. Straight chord displacement = 2R = 100 m; average velocity magnitude = 100 / (2.5*pi) = 40/pi ≈ 12.7 m/s.

B.diagnostic: Distance-displacement conflation: assumed average velocity magnitude equals average speed, neglecting that straight-line displacement (2R) is strictly shorter than curved arc path (pi*R).

C.diagnostic: Misapplied full-circuit zero displacement property to a half-revolution: average velocity vanishes only for a complete closed round trip (Delta r = 0), not a half-turn.

D.diagnostic: Inverted definitions: assigned chord displacement to speed and arc distance to velocity.

progressive_hints.title: Decisive Physical Invariant
progressive_hints.prompt_question: How do the definitions of average speed and average velocity differ for curvilinear motion?
progressive_hints.reveal_text: Average speed is total path distance divided by elapsed time ($v_{\text{avg}} = \frac{s}{\Delta t}$); average velocity is vector displacement divided by elapsed time ($\vec{v}_{\text{avg}} = \frac{\Delta \vec{r}}{\Delta t}$). In curved paths, $|\Delta \vec{r}| < s$, so $|\vec{v}_{\text{avg}}| < v_{\text{avg}}$.

progressive_hints.title: Geometric Representation
progressive_hints.prompt_question: What are the path distance and displacement magnitude for a half-circle of radius $R = 50.0\text{ m}$?
progressive_hints.reveal_text: Path distance is the semicircular arc: $s = \pi R = 50.0\pi\text{ m}$. Displacement magnitude is the straight diameter chord: $|\Delta \vec{r}| = 2R = 100.0\text{ m}$.

progressive_hints.title: First Mathematical Pivot
progressive_hints.prompt_question: What is the elapsed time at constant speed $v = 20.0\text{ m/s}$, and what are the resulting averages?
progressive_hints.reveal_text: Elapsed time $\Delta t = \frac{s}{v} = \frac{50.0\pi}{20.0} = 2.5\pi\text{ s}$. Average speed $= \frac{50.0\pi}{2.5\pi} = 20.0\text{ m/s}$. Average velocity magnitude $= \frac{100.0}{2.5\pi} = \frac{40.0}{\pi} \approx 12.7\text{ m/s}$.

reasoning_ladder.understand: Vehicle travels halfway around circular roundabout of radius $R = 50.0\text{ m}$ at constant speed $v = 20.0\text{ m/s}$. Goal: evaluate average speed and magnitude of average velocity vector.
reasoning_ladder.represent: Origin at roundabout center. Start at $A = (-R, 0)$, finish at $B = (+R, 0)$. Semicircular path length $s = \pi R$. Displacement vector $\Delta \vec{r} = \vec{r}_B - \vec{r}_A = 2R\hat{i}$.
reasoning_ladder.connect: Kinematic definitions: Average speed is scalar path length over time: $v_{\text{avg}} = \frac{s}{\Delta t}$. Average velocity is displacement vector over time: $\vec{v}_{\text{avg}} = \frac{\Delta \vec{r}}{\Delta t}$.
reasoning_ladder.calculate: Path distance: $s = 50.0\pi\text{ m}$. Elapsed time: $\Delta t = \frac{s}{v} = \frac{50.0\pi\text{ m}}{20.0\text{ m/s}} = 2.5\pi\text{ s}$. Average speed: $v_{\text{avg}} = \frac{50.0\pi}{2.5\pi} = 20.0\text{ m/s}$. Displacement: $|\Delta \vec{r}| = 2(50.0) = 100.0\text{ m}$. Average velocity magnitude: $|\vec{v}_{\text{avg}}| = \frac{100.0\text{ m}}{2.5\pi\text{ s}} = \frac{40.0}{\pi}\text{ m/s} \approx 12.73\text{ m/s}$.
reasoning_ladder.interpret: Because speed was constant along the path, average speed matches instantaneous speed ($20.0\text{ m/s}$). Because the direct chord is shorter than the arc by factor $2/\pi \approx 0.637$, the average velocity magnitude is only $12.7\text{ m/s}$.

derivation_steps: Elapsed time at constant speed: $\Delta t = \frac{s}{v} = \frac{50.0\pi\text{ m}}{20.0\text{ m/s}} = 2.5\pi\text{ s}$.
Average speed: $v_{\text{avg}} = \frac{s}{\Delta t} = \frac{50.0\pi\text{ m}}{2.5\pi\text{ s}} = 20.0\text{ m/s}$.
Average velocity magnitude: $|\vec{v}_{\text{avg}}| = \frac{|\Delta \vec{r}|}{\Delta t} = \frac{100.0\text{ m}}{2.5\pi\text{ s}} = \frac{40.0}{\pi}\text{ m/s} \approx 12.73\text{ m/s}$.

limiting_cases.expected: Delta r = 0 -> average velocity = 0 m/s; average speed = 20 m/s
Chord length approaches arc length -> |v_avg| approaches instantaneous speed 20 m/s

independent_check.quick_check: Ratio $|\vec{v}_{\text{avg}}| / v_{\text{avg}} = \frac{2R}{\pi R} = \frac{2}{\pi} \approx 0.6366$. $20.0 \times \frac{2}{\pi} = 12.73\text{ m/s}$. Exactly verified.
independent_check.check_it_another_way: Direct velocity component integration: With $\theta(t) = \omega t = \frac{v}{R} t$, the velocity components are $v_x(t) = -v\sin(\omega t)$ and $v_y(t) = v\cos(\omega t)$. The average $x$-velocity over $t \in [0, \pi/\omega]$ is $\frac{\omega}{\pi} \int_0^{\pi/\omega} v\sin(\omega t) dt = \frac{\omega v}{\pi} \left[-\frac{\cos(\omega t)}{\omega}\right]_0^{\pi/\omega} = \frac{2v}{\pi} = \frac{40}{\pi}\text{ m/s}$. Matches perfectly.
independent_check.watch_out: Do not equate average velocity with average speed; in all curved trajectories, $|\Delta \vec{r}| < s$, so $|\vec{v}_{\text{avg}}| < v_{\text{avg}}$.
independent_check.review_this_idea: Core 1: KIN-02 (Average Speed vs Average Velocity)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.stem: Raindrops are falling vertically downward at a terminal speed of $12\text{ m/s}$. A cyclist rides horizontally due East at a steady speed of $5\text{ m/s}$. At what angle to the vertical must the cyclist hold an umbrella to best protect themselves from the rain, and what is the relative speed of the raindrops with respect to the cyclist?

system_parameters.system_boundary: Raindrops and cyclist moving in vertical plane
idealizations: Vertical raindrop trajectory in ground frame

options.A: Relative Speed $= 13\text{ m/s}$, tilted at $\arctan(5/12) \approx 22.6^\circ$ toward the East
options.B: Relative Speed $= 13\text{ m/s}$, tilted at $\arctan(12/5) \approx 67.4^\circ$ toward the East
options.D: Relative Speed $= 17\text{ m/s}$, tilted at $45^\circ$ toward the West

qrt_contract.protected_work_W: Setting up the vector relative velocity equation v_rel = v_rain - v_cyclist and evaluating the resulting right-triangle magnitude and orientation angle.

rival_demands.rejection_rationale: Requires relative frame transformation and directional quadrant resolution, not direct scalar formula plugging.

A.diagnostic: Correct: v_rain = -12 j, v_cyclist = +5 i; v_rel = v_rain - v_cyclist = -5 i - 12 j. Speed = sqrt(5^2 + 12^2) = 13 m/s. Tilt angle with vertical = arctan(|v_x|/|v_y|) = arctan(5/12) ≈ 22.6° forward (East).

B.diagnostic: Inverted angle reference: evaluated tan(theta) = |v_y|/|v_x| = 12/5 = 67.4° relative to horizontal instead of vertical.

C.diagnostic: Subtracted speeds algebraically: 12 - 5 = 7 m/s, neglecting the perpendicular 2D vector geometry.

D.diagnostic: Added speeds algebraically: 12 + 5 = 17 m/s, and picked arbitrary 45° angle.

progressive_hints.title: Decisive Physical Invariant
progressive_hints.prompt_question: What is the defining vector equation relating raindrop velocity in the ground frame to that observed by the cyclist?
progressive_hints.reveal_text: The relative velocity of rain with respect to the cyclist is $\vec{v}_{\text{rel}} = \vec{v}_{\text{rain}} - \vec{v}_{\text{cyclist}}$. The umbrella must be aligned parallel to $\vec{v}_{\text{rel}}$ pointing opposite to the incoming drops.

progressive_hints.title: Cartesian Component Resolution
progressive_hints.prompt_question: What are the Cartesian vector components of $\vec{v}_{\text{rain}}$ and $\vec{v}_{\text{cyclist}}$ in the ground frame?
progressive_hints.reveal_text: Taking $+x$ East and $+y$ Upward: $\vec{v}_{\text{rain}} = -12\hat{j}\text{ m/s}$ and $\vec{v}_{\text{cyclist}} = +5\hat{i}\text{ m/s}$. Thus, $\vec{v}_{\text{rel}} = -5\hat{i} - 12\hat{j}\text{ m/s}$.

progressive_hints.title: First Mathematical Pivot
progressive_hints.prompt_question: What are the magnitude of $\vec{v}_{\text{rel}}$ and its tilt angle relative to the vertical?
progressive_hints.reveal_text: Magnitude: $|\vec{v}_{\text{rel}}| = \sqrt{(-5)^2 + (-12)^2} = \sqrt{25 + 144} = 13\text{ m/s}$. Tilt with vertical: $\tan\theta = \frac{|v_x|}{|v_y|} = \frac{5}{12} \implies \theta = \arctan(5/12) \approx 22.6^\circ$ tilted toward the East (into the wind).

reasoning_ladder.understand: Rain falls vertically at $12\text{ m/s}$, cyclist moves East at $5\text{ m/s}$. Goal: determine raindrop velocity relative to cyclist and required umbrella angle from vertical.
reasoning_ladder.represent: 2D Cartesian coordinate system with $+x$ East and $+y$ Upward. Vectors: $\vec{v}_r = -12\hat{j}$, $\vec{v}_c = 5\hat{i}$. Relative vector: $\vec{v}_{r/c} = \vec{v}_r - \vec{v}_c$.
reasoning_ladder.connect: Galilean relative velocity: $\vec{v}_{r/c} = \vec{v}_r - \vec{v}_c = -5\hat{i} - 12\hat{j}\text{ m/s}$.
reasoning_ladder.calculate: Magnitude: $v_{\text{rel}} = \sqrt{(-5)^2 + (-12)^2} = \sqrt{169} = 13\text{ m/s}$. Angle from vertical: $\tan\theta = \frac{|v_x|}{|v_y|} = \frac{5}{12} \approx 0.4167 \implies \theta = 22.6^\circ$. Direction: Rain appears to come from ahead and above, so umbrella points forward (East) at $22.6^\circ$ from vertical.
reasoning_ladder.interpret: To the moving cyclist, raindrops acquire an apparent westward horizontal velocity component of $-5\text{ m/s}$ alongside their downward $-12\text{ m/s}$, hitting at $13\text{ m/s}$ tilted $22.6^\circ$ forward.

derivation_steps: Establish reference frame: $\hat{i}$ pointing East, $\hat{j}$ pointing Upward.
Angle with vertical: $\tan\theta = \frac{v_c}{v_r} = \frac{5}{12} \implies \theta = \arctan(5/12) \approx 22.6^\circ$ tilted toward the East.

independent_check.quick_check: Pythagorean 5-12-13 integer triple: $5^2 + 12^2 = 25 + 144 = 169 = 13^2$. Exact integer match.
independent_check.check_it_another_way: Conservation of kinetic energy in relative transformation: $v_{\text{rel}}^2 = v_r^2 + v_c^2 - 2\vec{v}_r \cdot \vec{v}_c = 144 + 25 - 0 = 169 \implies v_{\text{rel}} = 13\text{ m/s}$. Verified.

questions.stem: A test vehicle starts from rest ($u = 0$) at $t = 0\text{ s}$ and experiences a triangular acceleration pulse as shown in Figure KIN-04. The acceleration increases linearly from $0$ to a maximum of $4\text{ m/s}^2$ at $t = 3\text{ s}$, then decreases linearly back to $0$ at $t = 6\text{ s}$. What is the final velocity of the vehicle at $t = 6\text{ s}$?

system_parameters.system_boundary: Test vehicle moving in 1D rectilinear trajectory

qrt_contract.protected_work_W: Evaluating the definite integral Delta v = int a dt as the triangular area under the acceleration-time graph: 1/2 * base * height.

rival_demands.rejection_rationale: Requires geometric calculus recognition that change in velocity equals graph area under variable acceleration pulse.

A.diagnostic: Correct: Delta v = Area under a-t curve = 1/2 * base * height = 1/2 * 6 * 4 = 12 m/s. Since u = 0, v(6) = 12 m/s.

B.diagnostic: Failed to multiply by 1/2: evaluated rectangular area base * height = 6 * 4 = 24 m/s.

C.diagnostic: Only integrated the first triangular half: 1/2 * 3 * 4 = 6 m/s, omitting the deceleration pulse from 3 to 6 s.

D.diagnostic: Averaged peak and base incorrectly: computed (3 + 6) * 4 / 2 = 18 m/s.

progressive_hints.title: Decisive Physical Invariant
progressive_hints.prompt_question: What physical quantity does the area under an acceleration-time graph represent?
progressive_hints.reveal_text: By the fundamental theorem of calculus, acceleration is $a = \frac{dv}{dt}$. Therefore, the area under the acceleration-time graph over an interval represents the change in velocity: $\Delta v = v(t_2) - v(t_1) = \int_{t_1}^{t_2} a(t) dt$.

progressive_hints.title: Geometric Representation
progressive_hints.prompt_question: What geometric shape does the acceleration-time graph form, and what are its dimensions?
progressive_hints.reveal_text: The graph forms a triangle with base along the time axis $b = 6\text{ s} - 0\text{ s} = 6\text{ s}$ and peak height along the acceleration axis $h = 4\text{ m/s}^2$ at $t = 3\text{ s}$.

progressive_hints.title: First Mathematical Pivot
progressive_hints.prompt_question: What is the area of this triangle, and what is the final velocity?
progressive_hints.reveal_text: Area $= \frac{1}{2} \times \text{base} \times \text{height} = \frac{1}{2} \times (6\text{ s}) \times (4\text{ m/s}^2) = 12\text{ m/s}$. Since $u = 0$, $v(6) = u + \Delta v = 0 + 12 = 12\text{ m/s}$.

reasoning_ladder.understand: Vehicle starts from rest at $t = 0$. $a(t)$ is triangular pulse from $0$ to $4\text{ m/s}^2$ at $3\text{ s}$, back to $0$ at $6\text{ s}$. Goal: find $v(6)$.
reasoning_ladder.represent: Acceleration graph $a(t)$ vs $t$. For $t \in [0, 3]$, $a(t) = \frac{4}{3}t$. For $t \in [3, 6]$, $a(t) = 4 - \frac{4}{3}(t-3) = 8 - \frac{4}{3}t$.
reasoning_ladder.connect: Kinematic relation: $dv = a(t) dt \implies v(6) - v(0) = \int_0^6 a(t) dt = \text{Area under } a(t) \text{ curve}$.
reasoning_ladder.calculate: Area of triangle: $\text{Area} = \frac{1}{2} \times \text{base} \times \text{height} = \frac{1}{2} \times 6\text{ s} \times 4\text{ m/s}^2 = 12\text{ m/s}$. Since $v(0) = 0$, $v(6) = 12\text{ m/s}$.
reasoning_ladder.interpret: Even though acceleration returned to zero at $t = 6\text{ s}$, the vehicle does NOT stop; it reaches its maximum constant cruising speed of $12\text{ m/s}$.

derivation_steps: Integrate both sides: $\Delta v = \int_0^6 a(t) dt$.
The definite integral corresponds exactly to the geometric area of the triangle on the $a-t$ plot.
Final velocity: $v(6) = v(0) + \Delta v = 0 + 12\text{ m/s} = 12\text{ m/s}$.

limiting_cases.condition: Pulse duration T -> 0 at fixed peak a_max

independent_check.quick_check: Average acceleration over the 6 seconds is $\bar{a} = \frac{1}{2} a_{\max} = 2\text{ m/s}^2$. Total velocity change: $\Delta v = \bar{a} \times \Delta t = 2 \times 6 = 12\text{ m/s}$. Exactly matches.
independent_check.check_it_another_way: Piecewise integration: Phase 1: $\int_0^3 \frac{4}{3}t dt = \left[ \frac{2}{3}t^2 \right]_0^3 = \frac{2}{3}(9) = 6\text{ m/s}$. Phase 2: $\int_3^6 (8 - \frac{4}{3}t) dt = \left[ 8t - \frac{2}{3}t^2 \right]_3^6 = (48 - 24) - (24 - 6) = 24 - 18 = 6\text{ m/s}$. Total $\Delta v = 6 + 6 = 12\text{ m/s}$.
independent_check.watch_out: Do NOT confuse the acceleration dropping to zero at $t = 6\text{ s}$ with the vehicle coming to rest; zero acceleration means constant velocity, not zero velocity.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.stem: Two projectiles are launched simultaneously from points on level ground separated by a horizontal distance $d = 100\text{ m}$. Particle 1 is launched from $(0, 0)$ with speed $u_1 = 20\text{ m/s}$ at an elevation angle of $30^\circ$. Particle 2 is launched from $(100\text{ m}, 0)$ toward Particle 1 with speed $u_2$ at an elevation angle of $30^\circ$ above the horizontal. Taking $g = 10\text{ m/s}^2$, what must be the speed $u_2$ for the two projectiles to collide in mid-air, and at what time $t$ after launch does the collision occur?

system_parameters.system_boundary: Two interacting projectiles in free fall
system_parameters.reference_frame: Inertial ground frame (+x from Particle 1 to Particle 2, +y upward)

qrt_contract.protected_work_W: Exploiting zero relative acceleration a_rel = 0 to establish equal vertical velocity matching u1y = u2y and solving for collision time.

rival_demands.rejection_rationale: Requires relative frame elimination of gravity and dual kinematic constraint coupling.

A.diagnostic: Correct: In the relative frame, relative acceleration is zero. For horizontal collision, vertical velocities must match: u1 sin 30 = u2 sin 30 => u2 = 20 m/s. Relative closing speed is u1 cos 30 + u2 cos 30 = 20*sqrt(3) m/s. Time = 100 / (20*sqrt(3)) = 5/sqrt(3) s ≈ 2.89 s.

B.diagnostic: Doubled u2 arbitrarily and used t = 5 s.

C.diagnostic: Computed u2 correctly but used t = d / u1 = 100 / 20 = 5 s ignoring particle 2's approach velocity.

D.diagnostic: Used horizontal component instead of total speed for u2.

progressive_hints.title: Decisive Physical Invariant
progressive_hints.prompt_question: What is the relative acceleration between two projectiles in free fall in the same uniform gravity field?
progressive_hints.reveal_text: Both particles experience identical downward gravitational acceleration: $\vec{a}_1 = -g\hat{j}$ and $\vec{a}_2 = -g\hat{j}$. Therefore, their relative acceleration is identically zero: $\vec{a}_{\text{rel}} = \vec{a}_1 - \vec{a}_2 = \vec{0}$. In the relative frame, each particle moves along a straight line at constant velocity!

progressive_hints.title: Geometric Collision Condition
progressive_hints.prompt_question: Since the particles start at the same ground elevation ($y_1(0) = y_2(0) = 0$), what must be the relationship between their vertical velocity components for them to collide?
progressive_hints.reveal_text: For the relative motion to stay along the horizontal line connecting them, the relative vertical velocity must vanish: $v_{y, \text{rel}} = u_1\sin 30^\circ - u_2\sin 30^\circ = 0 \implies u_2 = u_1 = 20\text{ m/s}$.

progressive_hints.title: First Mathematical Pivot
progressive_hints.prompt_question: What is the relative closing speed, and how long does it take to close the $100\text{ m}$ gap?
progressive_hints.reveal_text: The horizontal relative speed of approach is $v_{\text{close}} = u_1\cos 30^\circ + u_2\cos 30^\circ = 20\cos 30^\circ + 20\cos 30^\circ = 40\left(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right) = 20\sqrt{3}\text{ m/s}$. Collision time: $t = \frac{d}{v_{\text{close}}} = \frac{100}{20\sqrt{3}} = \frac{5}{\sqrt{3}}\text{ s} \approx 2.89\text{ s}$.

reasoning_ladder.understand: Particle 1 at $(0,0)$ launched at $30^\circ$ with $u_1 = 20\text{ m/s}$. Particle 2 at $(100,0)$ launched at $30^\circ$ toward Particle 1 with speed $u_2$. Goal: find $u_2$ and collision time $t$.
reasoning_ladder.represent: Inertial ground frame: $\vec{r}_1(t) = (u_1\cos\theta t)\hat{i} + (u_1\sin\theta t - \frac{1}{2}gt^2)\hat{j}$. $\vec{r}_2(t) = (d - u_2\cos\theta t)\hat{i} + (u_2\sin\theta t - \frac{1}{2}gt^2)\hat{j}$.
reasoning_ladder.connect: Relative frame transformation: $\vec{a}_{1/2} = \vec{g} - \vec{g} = \vec{0}$. Trajectory in relative frame is uniform straight line: $\Delta\vec{r}(t) = \Delta\vec{r}(0) + \vec{v}_{\text{rel}} t$.
reasoning_ladder.calculate: Vertical collision condition: $y_1(t) = y_2(t) \implies u_1\sin 30^\circ t = u_2\sin 30^\circ t \implies u_2 = u_1 = 20\text{ m/s}$. Horizontal collision condition: $x_1(t) = x_2(t) \implies u_1\cos 30^\circ t = d - u_2\cos 30^\circ t \implies (u_1 + u_2)\cos 30^\circ t = d$. Substitute: $40\left(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right) t = 100 \implies 20\sqrt{3} t = 100 \implies t = \frac{5}{\sqrt{3}}\text{ s} \approx 2.89\text{ s}$.
reasoning_ladder.interpret: Because both bodies fall together under gravity, the curvature cancels completely in the relative frame, reducing a complex 2D parabolic collision problem to simple 1D uniform straight-line relative motion.

derivation_steps: Vertical position match requires equal initial vertical velocity components: $u_1\sin 30^\circ = u_2\sin 30^\circ \implies u_2 = u_1 = 20\text{ m/s}$.
Horizontal relative velocity of approach: $v_{x, \text{rel}} = u_1\cos 30^\circ - (-u_2\cos 30^\circ) = 2(20\cos 30^\circ) = 20\sqrt{3}\text{ m/s}$.
Collision time: $t = \frac{d}{v_{x, \text{rel}}} = \frac{100\text{ m}}{20\sqrt{3}\text{ m/s}} = \frac{5}{\sqrt{3}}\text{ s} \approx 2.89\text{ s}$.

independent_check.quick_check: At $t = 5/\sqrt{3}\text{ s}$, $x_1 = 20\cos 30^\circ (5/\sqrt{3}) = 20(\sqrt{3}/2)(5/\sqrt{3}) = 50\text{ m}$. $x_2 = 100 - 50 = 50\text{ m}$. Coordinates match exactly at midpoint $x = 50\text{ m}$.
independent_check.check_it_another_way: Ground frame vertical match: $y_1(t) = 20(0.5)t - 5t^2 = 10t - 5t^2$. $y_2(t) = 20(0.5)t - 5t^2 = 10t - 5t^2$. Identical for all $t$, verifying collision at $x = 50\text{ m}$.
independent_check.watch_out: Do NOT attempt to solve quadratic equations in $t$ for both particles independently; transforming to the relative frame eliminates gravity instantly.
independent_check.review_this_idea: Core 1: KIN-10 (Relative Velocity & Common Acceleration Cancellation)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.stem: An ideal projectile is launched with speed $u$ at an elevation angle $\theta$ above the horizontal. In terms of $u, \theta,$ and $g$, what is the radius of curvature $\rho_{\text{apex}}$ of the parabolic trajectory at its highest point?

system_parameters.system_boundary: Ideal particle in free fall

qrt_contract.protected_work_W: Synthesizing normal centripetal acceleration a_n = v^2 / rho with apex kinematics v = u cos(theta) and normal acceleration a_n = g.

rival_demands.rejection_rationale: Requires connecting curvilinear osculating circle geometry with dynamic components.

A.diagnostic: Correct: At apex, velocity is strictly horizontal v = u*cos(theta), and acceleration is strictly perpendicular a_n = g. Centripetal relation: a_n = v^2 / rho => rho = v^2 / a_n = u^2*cos^2(theta) / g.

B.diagnostic: Used total launch speed u instead of apex velocity u*cos(theta): rho = u^2 / g.

C.diagnostic: Used vertical component u*sin(theta) instead of horizontal velocity u*cos(theta).

D.diagnostic: Divided by g*sin(theta) mistakenly assuming g must be resolved, when g is already purely perpendicular to the horizontal tangent.

progressive_hints.title: Decisive Physical Invariant
progressive_hints.prompt_question: What is the relationship between normal acceleration, speed, and the radius of curvature along any curved path?
progressive_hints.reveal_text: The normal (centripetal) acceleration perpendicular to the instantaneous velocity vector is given by $a_n = \frac{v^2}{\rho}$, where $v$ is the instantaneous speed and $\rho$ is the local radius of curvature.

progressive_hints.title: Kinematic State at Apex
progressive_hints.prompt_question: What are the magnitude and direction of the velocity and acceleration vectors at the projectile's apex?
progressive_hints.reveal_text: At the apex, vertical velocity vanishes ($v_y = 0$), so the velocity is purely horizontal: $v = v_x = u\cos\theta$. The acceleration is vertically downward: $\vec{a} = -g\hat{j}$, which is strictly perpendicular to the horizontal velocity vector!

progressive_hints.title: First Mathematical Pivot
progressive_hints.prompt_question: What is the resulting expression for $\rho_{\text{apex}}$?
progressive_hints.reveal_text: Since $\vec{a}$ is already perpendicular to $\vec{v}$, the full gravitational acceleration serves as the normal acceleration: $a_n = g$. Equating $g = \frac{(u\cos\theta)^2}{\rho_{\text{apex}}}$ yields $\rho_{\text{apex}} = \frac{u^2\cos^2\theta}{g}$.

reasoning_ladder.understand: Ideal projectile launched at angle $\theta$ with speed $u$. Goal: find the radius of curvature $\rho$ at the highest point (apex).
reasoning_ladder.represent: Intrinsic Frenet-Serret frame $(\hat{t}, \hat{n})$ at apex. Velocity vector is horizontal: $\vec{v} = (u\cos\theta)\hat{t}$. Acceleration vector is vertical: $\vec{a} = g\hat{n}$.
reasoning_ladder.connect: Curvilinear kinematic relation: $a_n = \frac{v^2}{\rho}$. Here, $a_n = g$ and $v = u\cos\theta$.
reasoning_ladder.calculate: Substitute: $g = \frac{(u\cos\theta)^2}{\rho_{\text{apex}}} \implies \rho_{\text{apex}} = \frac{u^2\cos^2\theta}{g}$.
reasoning_ladder.interpret: As launch angle $\theta$ increases toward $90^\circ$ (vertical throw), apex horizontal speed vanishes and the parabola degenerates into a straight spike with zero radius of curvature.

derivation_steps: Instantaneous speed at apex: $v_{\text{apex}} = u_x = u\cos\theta$.
Since velocity is along $\hat{i}$, $\vec{a}$ is entirely perpendicular to the velocity: $a_n = g$.

limiting_cases.expected: rho -> u^2 / g (Standard osculating circle of flat parabola)
rho -> 0 (Trajectory degenerates into a 1D vertical line)

independent_check.quick_check: From differential geometry: $\rho = \frac{(1 + (y')^2)^{3/2}}{|y''|}$. At apex, $y' = 0$, so $\rho = \frac{1}{|y''|}$. For parabola $y = x\tan\theta - \frac{g x^2}{2u^2\cos^2\theta}$, $y'' = -\frac{g}{u^2\cos^2\theta}$. Thus $\rho = \frac{1}{g/(u^2\cos^2\theta)} = \frac{u^2\cos^2\theta}{g}$. Matches identically.
independent_check.check_it_another_way: At $\theta = 45^\circ$, $\rho = \frac{u^2(1/2)}{g} = \frac{u^2}{2g} = H_{\max}$. The radius of curvature at the apex of a $45^\circ$ projectile equals its maximum height. Physically sound.
independent_check.watch_out: Do NOT resolve $g$ with $\cos\theta$ at the apex; velocity is horizontal, so the entire vertical vector $g$ is already perpendicular.
independent_check.review_this_idea: Core 1: KIN-08 (2D Projectile Component Decoupling)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.stem: The position of a particle moving along the x-axis is given by $x(t) = t^3 - 6t^2 + 9t$, where $x$ is in meters and $t$ is in seconds (Figure KIN-05). During which of the following time intervals is the particle moving in the negative direction while speeding up?

system_parameters.system_boundary: Single particle moving along 1D axis

qrt_contract.protected_work_W: Differentiating position to obtain v(t) = 3(t-1)(t-3) and a(t) = 6(t-2), and finding the intersection where v(t) < 0 and a(t) < 0.

rival_demands.rejection_rationale: Requires dynamic sign analysis and simultaneous sign concordance modeling for direction vs speed change.

A.diagnostic: Correct: v(t) = 3(t-1)(t-3) < 0 for 1 < t < 3 (moving in negative direction). a(t) = 6(t-2) < 0 for t < 2. Speeding up in negative direction requires v and a to have the same negative sign: intersection is 1 < t < 2 s.

B.diagnostic: For 0 < t < 1, v(t) > 0 and a(t) < 0: particle is moving in POSITIVE direction while SLOWING DOWN.

C.diagnostic: For 2 < t < 3, v(t) < 0 but a(t) > 0: signs oppose, so the particle is SLOWING DOWN while moving in negative direction.

D.diagnostic: For t > 3, v(t) > 0 and a(t) > 0: particle is speeding up, but in the POSITIVE direction.

progressive_hints.title: Decisive Physical Invariant
progressive_hints.prompt_question: What mathematical conditions on velocity $v(t)$ and acceleration $a(t)$ define 'moving in the negative direction' and 'speeding up'?
progressive_hints.reveal_text: Moving in the negative direction means $v(t) < 0$. Speeding up means speed $|v(t)|$ is increasing, which occurs if and only if velocity and acceleration have the SAME SIGN. Therefore, moving in the negative direction while speeding up requires BOTH $v(t) < 0$ AND $a(t) < 0$!

progressive_hints.title: Calculus Representation
progressive_hints.prompt_question: What are the algebraic expressions for $v(t)$ and $a(t)$ by differentiating $x(t) = t^3 - 6t^2 + 9t$?
progressive_hints.reveal_text: $v(t) = \frac{dx}{dt} = 3t^2 - 12t + 9 = 3(t-1)(t-3)$. Acceleration: $a(t) = \frac{dv}{dt} = 6t - 12 = 6(t-2)$.

progressive_hints.title: First Mathematical Pivot
progressive_hints.prompt_question: What is the common interval of $t$ where both $v(t) < 0$ and $a(t) < 0$?
progressive_hints.reveal_text: $v(t) < 0 \implies (t-1)(t-3) < 0 \implies 1 < t < 3\text{ s}$. $a(t) < 0 \implies 6(t-2) < 0 \implies t < 2\text{ s}$. The intersection of $(1, 3)$ and $(-\infty, 2)$ is $1\text{ s} < t < 2\text{ s}$.

reasoning_ladder.understand: Particle position $x(t) = t^3 - 6t^2 + 9t$. Goal: identify time interval where particle moves in negative direction and speeds up.
reasoning_ladder.represent: Differentiate: $v(t) = 3(t-1)(t-3)$ and $a(t) = 6(t-2)$. Real number line partitioned by roots $t = 1, 2, 3$.
reasoning_ladder.connect: Direction is determined by sign of $v(t)$: negative direction $\iff v(t) < 0$. Rate of change of speed: $\frac{d}{dt}(v^2) = 2 v a$. Speed increases $\iff v(t) a(t) > 0$. Combined condition: $v(t) < 0$ and $a(t) < 0$.
reasoning_ladder.calculate: 1) $v(t) < 0 \implies 1 < t < 3$. 2) $a(t) < 0 \implies t < 2$. Overlapping interval: $1\text{ s} < t < 2\text{ s}$.
reasoning_ladder.interpret: At $t = 1\text{ s}$, the particle halts momentarily at $x = 4\text{ m}$ and starts accelerating in the negative direction, reaching peak negative speed at the inflection point $t = 2\text{ s}$ where $a = 0$.

derivation_steps: Condition for motion in negative direction: $v(t) < 0 \implies 1 < t < 3$.
Condition for speeding up: $a(t)$ must have the same sign as $v(t)$, so $a(t) < 0 \implies 6t - 12 < 0 \implies t < 2$.
Intersection of conditions: $t \in (1, 3) \cap (-\infty, 2) = (1, 2)$, which is $1\text{ s} < t < 2\text{ s}$.

limiting_cases.expected: v(1.5) = 3(0.5)(-1.5) = -2.25 m/s < 0, a(1.5) = 6(1.5 - 2) = -3 m/s² < 0. Both negative => Speeding up in negative direction!

independent_check.quick_check: At $t = 1\text{ s}$, speed is $|v(1)| = 0\text{ m/s}$. At $t = 2\text{ s}$, speed is $|v(2)| = |3(1)(-1)| = 3\text{ m/s}$. Speed strictly increased from $0$ to $3\text{ m/s}$ in negative direction. Verified.
independent_check.check_it_another_way: Graph of $x(t)$: local maximum at $t=1$ ($x=4\text{ m}$), inflection point at $t=2$ ($x=2\text{ m}$), local minimum at $t=3$ ($x=0\text{ m}$). Between $t=1$ and $t=2$, curve is concave down ($a < 0$) and downward sloping ($v < 0$). Exactly matches.
independent_check.watch_out: Do NOT equate 'negative acceleration' with 'slowing down'; negative acceleration speeds up any object already moving in the negative direction.
independent_check.review_this_idea: Core 1: KIN-04 (Signs, Direction & Acceleration Reversal)
